Subdivision flags in a text column, as ISO 3166-2 codes

Source: R/emoji-flags.R
emoji_subdivision.Rd

emoji_subdivision() returns one row per subdivision flag in the text (the flags of England, Scotland and Wales, and any other tag sequence of the same shape), with the code its tag characters spell ("GB-SCT") and, for the three Unicode recommends, the name.

Usage

emoji_subdivision(data, text)

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble containing a text column. Grouped data frames are accepted. The verbs that work a row at a time (adding columns, or keeping and expanding rows) carry the grouping through to their result, as dplyr::mutate() and dplyr::filter() do. The verbs that pool across rows – the counts, the co-occurrence edge lists, the time series – warn that they ignore the grouping and return one corpus-wide answer.

text

The text column to scan, supplied unquoted. Any atomic column is accepted and read as character, so a factor works and a numeric, Date or logical one simply contains no emoji. A list column – or a data-frame column – is refused rather than coerced, because coercing one deparses it and the emoji found would be in the code rather than in your data. What counts as an emoji is the same in every verb; see the Detection section of tidyEmoji for the one case that surprises people, code points that are emoji only when they carry U+FE0F.

Value

A tibble with the columns of data plus .emoji (the whole tag sequence), .emoji_subdivision (the ISO 3166-2 code its tags spell) and .emoji_subdivision_name (the Unicode name for the three in the catalogue, NA otherwise). One row per sequence, in reading order; rows without one are dropped.

Details

A subdivision flag is not a regional-indicator pair. It is a black flag (U+1F3F4) followed by invisible tag characters spelling a subdivision code in lower case, and a cancel tag (U+E007F): Scotland is the black flag, then g b s c t, then the cancel tag. The code is therefore read straight off the tags, for any well-formed sequence.

Only three such sequences are in the catalogue, GB-ENG, GB-SCT and GB-WLS, and only those three are emoji the other verbs count. Any other (US-TX spelled the same way, say) is valid Unicode that no major platform draws as a flag, so it is reported here with its code and NA for the name, while emoji_frequency() and the rest see only the black flag at its start. That is the honest answer to a question the text does not settle: the sender typed a Texas flag and the reader most likely saw a black one.

See also

emoji_country() for country flags; emoji_flag() to convert.

Examples

scotland <- intToUtf8(c(0x1F3F4, 0xE0067, 0xE0062, 0xE0073, 0xE0063,
                        0xE0074, 0xE007F))
df <- data.frame(text = c(paste("go", scotland), "none"))
emoji_subdivision(df, text)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   text  .emoji .emoji_subdivision .emoji_subdivision_name
#>   <chr> <chr>  <chr>              <chr>                  
#> 1 go 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿     GB-SCT             Scotland
